feedback: If the learner expects the colour to stay only at the base, point to the dye in the leaf veins or petals: water climbed all the way up. Trace the continuous path base to stem to leaf together.
If the learner expects the stem to get wet on the outside, cut it crossways and show the coloured dots inside: water travels inside through specific channels, not over the surface.
If the learner expects an instant result, prompt 'what will you look at, and when?' so they build in waiting and a before/after comparison; the process takes hours.
If the learner says the flower is 'making' the colour, remind them the beaker water was dyed and that same colour has now arrived in the petals: it was carried there.
activities.intendedInsight: Water is drawn upward from the base of the plant, through fine tubes inside the stem, all the way up to the leaves and flowers. Watching dyed water appear at the top is the evidence that this invisible, slow process happens.
learnerActions: Stand a stick of white celery with leaves on, or a pale white carnation, in a beaker of water dyed a bright colour (e.g. red or blue).
Before leaving it, write or say your plan: what will you look at, and when? Set up a before/after comparison and take a first photo or drawing.
Over several hours (or leave overnight), record what you see at intervals with photos or drawings, so the slow upward creep of colour is captured as evidence, not just a final result.
When the colour has risen, point out where the dye ended up (in the leaf veins / petals) and describe which way the water travelled.
Cut across the stem with scissors or a knife (with adult help) and use a hand lens to find the coloured dots or lines inside, the tiny tubes that carried the water.
Draw and label a diagram showing the path of the water: base/roots to stem to leaves and flowers.
activities.title: Real coloured-water investigation (celery or white flower)

feedback: If a learner orders observation before set-up, remind them you cannot observe before you have set it up and waited.
If a learner says water moves down or in all directions, point back to the dye reaching the top leaves/petals as evidence of an upward route.
If a learner predicts a single colour for the split stem, explain each half carries up its own dye, so the flower usually shows two tones, often in different parts of the petals.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state the direction of movement (upward), the ordered pathway, and the role of the internal tubes, and can predict a variation.
learnerActions: Put the investigation steps in the right order (set up specimen in dyed water, record over time, observe the colour risen, slice the stem to see the tubes).
Draw the water's route on a plant outline from base to stem to leaves.
Answer: which way does water move through the plant, and where does the colour appear first and last?
Predict: if you split the stem and stand each half in a different colour, what will the flower look like?
activities.title: Check understanding of method and pathway
